title: The Dust Tail Hubble Just Photographed
idea: Hubble photographs, in visible light, a long tail of dark fluffy dust around the young star Beta Pictoris, 63 light-years away; what it is and what is still unknown

cast.name: Mia
cast.look: young stargazer in a green scarf, round glasses, a notebook in her hand

scenes.title: A tail around a star
scenes.place: A hilltop at night under a huge starry sky, Mia sits on the grass with a notebook and a small telescope

lines.t: Sixty-three light-years away, a young star is trailing a tail of dust.
Reported on the eleventh of November, from a study in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.
The star is called Beta Pictoris. And now Hubble has photographed the tail in ordinary visible light.
A tail of dust? Around a star?

scenes.title: Webb saw it first
scenes.place: A dark observatory control room with glowing screens, a big telescope dome seen through the window

lines.t: The tail has a nickname: the Cat's Tail.
The James Webb telescope found it in twenty twenty-four, but only in mid-infrared light.
In visible light it was almost invisible, because the dust is very dark.
So why could Hubble see it at all?

scenes.title: Six looks
scenes.place: A hilltop at night under a huge starry sky, a drawing of the Hubble telescope and a long dusty tail on Mia's notebook page

lines.t: Patience. Hubble looked at the system six times, between twenty twelve and twenty twenty-five.
Its long exposures pulled out the faint glow of light scattered by the dust.
Together with the Webb data, they suggest the tail lies mostly flat across our view, not pointing toward us.
Earlier estimates said it could stretch up to a thousand astronomical units. About ninety-three billion miles.

scenes.title: Fluffy and dark
scenes.place: A close view of a notebook page on a hilltop at night, a drawing of a single tiny dust grain with holes in it

lines.t: The dust is made mostly of carbon-rich material. Each grain is about one micron across.
The grains look porous and fluffy, a bit like tiny sponges, and they soak up most of the light.
Where would so much fluffy dust come from?

scenes.title: What we do not know
scenes.place: A hilltop at night under a huge starry sky, Mia looks up at the stars with her notebook closed

lines.t: One idea: a collision between two bodies the size of Pluto, that made carbon vapor, which cooled into fluffy grains.
The authors say this is uncertain. It fits the evidence, but it needs more observations to confirm.
And this is one young star. It does not show that our own young solar system had the same tail.
If a figure here is out of date, the sources in the description are the reference.
So what would you want Hubble and Webb to look at next?
